title: Minimum Operations to Make the Array K-Increasing
statement:
You get an array `arr` of `n` positive integers (indexed from 0) and a positive integer `k`. Call `arr` *K-increasing* when `arr[i - k] <= arr[i]` for every index `i` with `k <= i <= n - 1`.

One operation picks any index `i` and overwrites `arr[i]` with any positive integer you like. Return the smallest number of operations that makes `arr` K-increasing for the given `k`.
notes:
## Intuition

The rule `arr[i - k] <= arr[i]` only ever links indices that share the same remainder modulo `k`. So the array splits into `k` independent chains: indices `start, start + k, start + 2k, ...`. Each chain must end up non-decreasing, and the chains never interact.

Inside one chain, the values we leave alone must already be non-decreasing; everything else can be rewritten to fit around them (any positive integer is allowed). So the fewest changes for a chain is its length minus its **longest non-decreasing subsequence**. Trying every subset of kept values is exponential, and the O(m²) DP is too slow for 10^5 values, so we use the patience-sorting LIS with binary search.

## Approach

1. For each `start` from `0` to `k - 1`, walk the chain `i = start, start + k, ...`.
2. Keep `tails`, where `tails[j]` is the smallest possible last value of a non-decreasing subsequence of length `j + 1`.
3. For each `value`, binary-search the first position whose tail is **strictly greater** than `value` and put `value` there (this appends when no such tail exists).
4. Count the chain's `length`; the chain needs `length - tails.length` changes. Add that to `operations`.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [5,4,3,2,1]`, `k = 1`, so there is one chain holding all five values. `5` makes `tails = [5]`; `4` replaces it (`[4]`), then `3`, `2` and `1` each replace position 0 too. The chain has `length = 5` and `tails.length = 1`, so `operations = 5 - 1 = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): every index is visited once, with a binary search over `tails`.
- Space: O(n / k) for the `tails` of the current chain.

## Pitfalls

- The order is non-decreasing, so equal values may stay: search for the first tail `> value`, not `>= value`, or `[2,2,2]` would wrongly need changes.
- Forgetting to split by remainder and running one LIS over the whole array solves a different problem.
- An O(m²) LIS per chain times out when `k = 1` and `n = 10^5`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `operations` | total changes needed over all chains |
| `start` | first index of the current chain |
| `tails` | smallest tail for each subsequence length in this chain |
| `length` | number of values in this chain |
| `value` | the chain value being placed |
| `left`, `right`, `mid` | binary-search bounds |

narration.2: Count the changes needed across all chains.
narration.3: Each remainder start in 0..k-1 begins its own independent chain.
narration.4: tails[j] holds the smallest last value of a non-decreasing run of length j + 1 in this chain.
narration.6: Walk the chain by jumping k positions at a time.
narration.10: Binary-search tails for the first entry that is strictly greater than value.
narration.12: A tail equal to or below value can be extended, so search to the right of it.
narration.15: This tail is bigger than value, so the answer is here or further left.
narration.18: Put value at that position: it either extends the longest run or lowers a tail.
narration.19: Count one more value in this chain.
narration.21: Values outside the longest non-decreasing run must be changed, so add the difference.
narration.23: Return the total number of changes over all k chains.
